title: Humphry Davy Opposes Faraday
text:
In 1812 Michael Faraday, a young bookbinder's apprentice in London with almost no schooling, attended lectures by Sir Humphry Davy, the most famous chemist in Britain. He wrote out his notes, bound them and sent them to Davy, asking for work. In 1813 Davy hired him as a laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution and soon took him on a long tour of Europe. Faraday learned fast.

By the early 1820s the assistant was making discoveries of his own: the first electric motor in 1821 and, in 1823, the liquefaction of chlorine. Davy, who had suggested the chlorine experiment, felt Faraday did not give him enough credit.

In 1823 friends nominated Faraday for Fellowship of the Royal Society. Davy was its President, and he opposed the election. He told Faraday to take down the certificate. Faraday replied that he had not put it up and could not take it down; his proposers had. In January 1824 Faraday was elected, with a single vote against him.

Faraday never spoke ill of his old patron. He went on to become one of the greatest experimental scientists in history.
lesson: Be glad when someone you trained begins to surpass you. A mentor's envy can turn a proud achievement into a sour rivalry.
location: Royal Institution and Royal Society, London, England
source: Faraday's correspondence; Henry Bence Jones, The Life and Letters of Faraday (1870)
caveat: Some details, such as the single vote against, rest on later accounts, and Davy's motives are interpreted differently by historians.
